result.rationale: Artifact A is a generic template shell (including an unfilled {{title}} token) whose every line is DoD-style boilerplate ('appropriate manner,' 'as needed'); it answers none of the five probes and cannot be used to scope work. Artifacts B and C are both specific, numerically grounded, and free of the four planted distractor facts (OS versions, marketing campaign, microservices ownership, Legal/joint-account note), so neither wins or loses on padding. The deciding difference is substantive: the scenario's central ask was an airtight treatment of the estimated-authorization-then-settlement edge case, and Artifact B names that edge case but never actually resolves it (the bullet is circular: 'the criteria specify how...' without saying how), which fails retrieval probe 2 and undercuts the one thing the requester most cared about. Artifact C resolves that same case explicitly across two linked criteria (decline at authorization if it would exceed; do not retroactively decline at settlement, log and surface as informational) and goes further by flagging that this is the story's known pain point rather than an assumption, and by surfacing one genuine open question (mid-period limit change re-evaluation) as a decision for product rather than quietly picking an answer. That is exactly the decision-vs-told and scopeable-without-meeting behavior the held-out criteria are checking for, and it is why C's held-out mean pulls further ahead of B's than the rubric mean alone would suggest, consistent with the eval's own circularity check (a large rubric gap next to a comparatively larger held-out gap here signals a genuine document-quality difference, not template-teaches-rubric). result.rationale: Scored each artifact against the rubric's six criteria and the four held-out decision-usefulness criteria independently, using the anchor scale (5 reserved for untouchable work, ties broken downward), then separately verified each of the scenario's five retrieval probes could be answered from that document alone, and checked both documents against the three named distractor facts (button color, Java/Kotlin refactor, marketing campaign) -- neither included any, so no penalty applied there. Applied the anti-form instruction by scoring content substance over structure - Artifact B's narrative, less-checklisted format was not penalized in itself (its held-out scores are actually higher than A's), but its genuine missing content (edge cases, non-functional bars) was penalized on the relevant rubric cells regardless of how organized the rest of the document looked. Checked both documents against the scenario's three distractor facts (brand teal color, Java-to-Kotlin backend refactor, Family Pilot marketing campaign) - neither artifact included any of them, so no penalty applied either direction. Held ties to the lower score per the anchor-scale instruction where genuinely torn (e.g., A's single-behavior-scenarios criterion, where the letter of the rubric is violated by all three dedicated GWT scenarios despite the outcomes being closely related).

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Every section is templated filler with the specific facts sanded off: no timestamps, no numbers, no named evidence, no real owners or tickets ('The appropriate team', 'To be determined'). Impact table literally reads 'A subset of users... for a period of time... noticeable' with zero checkable figures. Timeline entries are 'Early in the sequence of events' / 'Shortly thereafter' rather than any UTC time. Root Causes offer no evidence, just restated generality. Trigger cites a vague 'threshold the team generally uses' with no pointer to where it was published. None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document; nothing about the 02:14 failure, the stale alert route, the failed failover, the VP's 48-hour ask, or the ownership gap survives. On held-out criteria it is uninformative rather than actively contradictory, so no_internal_contradiction is trivially true but empty; the rest score floor. This is organized like a postmortem and contains none of the content of one.

artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: Strongest on checkable specifics: every impact row, timeline entry (bar one 'Later that morning'), and root cause carries a real number or named piece of evidence, and root causes correctly avoid pinning blame on the departed engineer or the non-owner who ran the failover. Cleanly avoids both distractors (no $42k cost figure, no reconciliation-migration detail beyond what's needed to answer the ask via an action item). All five probes answerable, including the VP/48-hour question via the 'assess... report to VP within 48 hours' action item. Two real gaps: Trigger restates thresholds ('meets the team's threshold for user-visible downtime') without citing where any such criterion was published beforehand, so it reads as a borrowed generic list dressed in this incident's numbers; and every action item's Ticket field is literally 'TBD' with Status 'Not started', so despite naming role-owners, none of these are actually tracked outside the document as the criterion requires. On held-out: no stated stop/rollback/escalation condition anywhere, and the narrative voice mostly flattens observed fact and author judgment together rather than separating them (e.g. root-cause claims about what the failover procedure 'lacks' are asserted, not marked as inference).

artifacts.label: Artifact C
artifacts.notes: Best on decision-usefulness: explicitly flags what is observed record versus the author's own inference ('this is the best current explanation, not a verified one'), states a real escalation threshold ('after the second SLA miss in six months, the incident automatically escalates to VP-level review'), and directly reasons through the VP's actual question rather than deferring it to an action item, while being honest that the final call belongs to the VP. Avoids both distractors (no cost figure; references the migration only insofar as the ask requires answering the VP's question, without importing the next-quarter scheduling detail). But it is weak on the rubric fundamentals: there is no Trigger section at all, so nothing points to a pre-published criterion; the Recommended Changes are prose bullets with zero named owners and zero ticket IDs anywhere, worse than Artifact B's placeholder tracking; the opening incident line ('01:40 to ~06:00+90min UTC') does not arithmetically reconcile with the Impact section's stated 6h40m delay, a checkable internal inconsistency; and 'What happened' doesn't carry impact magnitude or a clear resolved/not-resolved statement in one place, so it doesn't fully stand alone the way the criterion wants. Four of five probes answered; the 48-hour deadline for the VP's decision is never stated anywhere in the document, so that probe fails on this document alone even though 'the VP decides' is well covered.

result.strongest: Artifact B, by a narrow margin over Artifact C, with Artifact A a distant last.
result.rationale:
Artifact A is content-free templating: every field that should carry a checkable fact (a timestamp, a number, an owner, a ticket, a cited trigger criterion) is replaced with a placeholder phrase, so zero of the five probes are answerable and it scores at or near floor on every rubric and held-out criterion alike. It is disqualified on substance, not on tone.

Artifacts B and C are both clearly working from the same real incident facts, both avoid the two planted distractors (the $42k cost figure and the reconciliation-migration scheduling detail), and both are far more useful than A. They fail in different places. B is stronger on the rubric criteria that were taught to the treatment arm: fully checkable impact and timeline numbers, evidenced root causes that don't name a person, and full retrieval-probe recall (5/5). Its two real weaknesses are a Trigger section that restates generic thresholds without citing where they were published, and an Action Items table whose owners are real roles but whose tickets are uniformly 'TBD' -- so nothing is actually trackable outside the document yet. C is stronger on the held-out, harder-to-fake criteria: it is the only artifact that visibly separates what the author was told from what the author concluded, it states a genuine escalation/kill threshold, and it directly engages the VP's actual decision rather than parking it in a future action item. But C pays for that with real rubric losses that matter operationally: no Trigger section at all, literally no named owner or ticket anywhere in its recommended changes, one fewer probe answered (the 48-hour deadline is never stated), and an internal arithmetic inconsistency between its opening time span and its own Impact section. Because a postmortem's job is to be both honest and actionable-without-a-meeting, and C sacrifices trackability entirely while B only weakens it, B edges out as the marginally stronger document overall, with both landing at the same holistic tier: real, specific, distractor-free work that a senior practitioner would still send back for concrete fixes (name the trigger source and file real tickets, in B's case; add a trigger section and assign real owners, in C's case) rather than ship as-is.

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Strong on epistemic labeling (Confirmed/Unconfirmed/Unresolved tags let a reader cleanly separate what was observed from what is theorized - this is the document's best feature and drives a high decision_vs_information score). All 5 probes answerable: no root cause asserted, both duration figures given, February relation explicitly called an open question, CDN SLA miss stated (35 vs 15 min), Android update explicitly neither ruled in nor out. But it fails two rubric criteria badly: there is no Trigger section at all (nothing names a pre-published threshold that made this postmortem-worthy), and the action items have no owners, no ticket IDs, and no status field ('Owner and target date to be assigned at the exec meeting' is a placeholder, not tracking). The 'What happened' section also defers cause status entirely to a later section, so it does not stand alone per the rubric's literal requirement. Most consequentially, it contains a dedicated section naming the three scenario distractors (social sentiment, billing incident, churn data) in order to exclude them - this still surfaces topics the scenario explicitly flags as not belonging in a document of this type, and per the eval's anti-distractor instruction that counts against completeness/discipline, not for it. No stop/rollback/kill condition is stated anywhere.

artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: Summary section is the strongest instance of summary_stands_alone across the two: cause status, both duration figures, and explicit resolution state ('The incident is resolved. Root cause is not confirmed...') are all co-located, satisfying the rubric criterion literally rather than deferring cause elsewhere. Has an explicit Timeline table with clock-time estimates (while honestly flagging they are not yet reconciled against logs) and a Trigger section that names the specific threshold values met, though it admits it cannot yet cite where those criteria were published - a real but partial attempt, better than Artifact A's total absence of a Trigger section. Action items carry named owners and a status column, but every ticket field reads 'TBD', so actions_are_tracked is only half-satisfied (owner+status present, no real ticket ID as the rubric requires). All 5 probes answerable directly and correctly: no confirmed cause, both durations, February relation explicitly unresolved, SLA miss stated, Android update explicitly neither ruled in nor out. Contains zero mention of any of the three scenario distractors, which is a real discipline advantage over Artifact A given the eval's explicit instruction to penalize inclusion of those facts. No stop/rollback/kill condition is stated anywhere, same gap as Artifact A. The gain over Artifact A here is substantive content (a real summary that stands alone, a timeline with checkable timestamps, an attempted trigger citation, tracked owners/status) rather than mere formatting, so it is not simply rewarded for looking organized.

result.rationale: Both documents are honest about the unconfirmed root cause and both answer all five retrieval probes correctly, so neither loses ground on the eval's core no-overclaiming requirement. The separation comes from the rubric criteria: Artifact B's Summary section literally co-locates cause status, duration, and resolution state (Artifact A's equivalent section omits cause entirely and defers it), B attempts a Trigger citation where A has none, B's Timeline gives checkable clock-time estimates where A gives only relative durations, and B's action items carry named owners and a status column where A's carry neither (both fall short of real ticket IDs, so actions_are_tracked is a genuine gap for both, worse for A). On held-out criteria the two are tied: both distinguish observation from theory reasonably well, both are internally consistent, and neither states a stop/rollback/kill condition. The deciding factor beyond the rubric numbers is discipline: Artifact A devotes a full section to naming the scenario's three distractor facts (social sentiment, the unrelated billing incident, pending churn data) in order to declare them out of scope, which still surfaces content the eval explicitly instructs judges to penalize; Artifact B never raises any of them. B's structural advantages here reflect actual added information (a stand-alone summary, real timestamps, tracked owners) rather than cosmetic organization, so rewarding it does not violate the anti-form instruction.

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Rubric per-criterion: problem_weight_and_evidence=4 (Context+Problem sections together, including the 40%/$18/22-min figures and the FTE shortfall, outweigh the Solution overview; evidence is real but split across two sections rather than concentrated in one, which is the nitpick). goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=4 (two clean outcome goals plus a date goal; non-goals give reasons, though the kiosk one is stronger-reasoned than the voice-to-text one). target_user_specificity=4 (names primary/secondary segments with percentages and situations - 72% of 214 surveyed prefer phone/tablet, 35% of 65+ need staffed fallback - plus front desk/billing as internal users). metrics_primary_and_guardrail=4 (explicit Primary / Guardrail / Measurement window labels, textbook shape). open_questions_owned_and_dated=4 (three rows, each with a named owner and a milestone-based needed-by date, no TBDs). unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=3 (FR table has a MoSCoW column on every row, but UX and design gives only one edge case, not a full empty/loading/error triad). Held-out: scopable_without_a_meeting=4 (FR/NFR/Dependencies tables carry owner and status, including an honestly-flagged 'needs confirmation' row). explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=4 (guardrail plus an explicit rollback clause in the rollout plan). no_internal_contradiction=3 (FR-3 asserts Epic integration as a flat 'Must' while Open Questions still lists Epic-vs-athenahealth as unresolved and needed before build - a real, pointable tension, softened but not eliminated by the Solution overview's 'pending confirmation' hedge). decision_vs_input_traceable=4 (explicitly narrates that the ops director's newer verbal direction supersedes the June email, and that Carla Nguyen, not the medical director, owns sequencing). artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: Rubric per-criterion: problem_weight_and_evidence=4 (all the quantified evidence - 22 min, 40%, $18, Denise Ruiz by name, the Riverside FTE gap - sits concentrated in one dense Problem section). goals_measurable_nongoals_explicit=3 (three well-phrased outcome goals with numeric thresholds, but the Out-of-scope list spends a full paragraph each on GDPR and the no-show claim - two of the scenario's three named distractors, reproduced almost verbatim - which is exactly the over-inclusion the task instructions say to penalize, not credit as thoroughness). target_user_specificity=2 (no Target users section exists at all; the 72%/35% figures appear only inside Scope as a feature justification, not as a named 'who is this for' segment with their situation - a reader cannot point to the section the criterion asks for). metrics_primary_and_guardrail=3 (three goal metrics are listed as coequals and the kill-criterion prose only afterward singles out two of them as the go/no-go pair; nothing is labeled 'primary' vs 'guardrail' the way the criterion expects, so a reader has to infer the split). open_questions_owned_and_dated=2 (no Open questions section exists; owner/timing information for the EHR conflict and the budget decision is embedded in Risks-and-unknowns prose without a dated needed-by). unhappy_paths_and_prioritized_requirements=1 (no functional requirements list of any kind, so nothing carries a MoSCoW marker, and no UX/design section, so there are no empty, loading, or error states - this is the criterion's clearest failure mode, not a partial credit case). Held-out: scopable_without_a_meeting=2 (no FR/dependency table with owner+status; an engineer would need to extract build items from narrative paragraphs and would still need to ask who owns closing the $16k hardware gap). explicit_stop_or_kill_condition=4 (states the kill criterion in bold and names it as such - very explicit). no_internal_contradiction=4 (consistently caveats the Epic/athenahealth conflict everywhere it appears, no flat assertion contradicting a still-open question). decision_vs_input_traceable=4 (explains its reasoning, not just its conclusion - e.g. 'IT owns the technical integration decision' as the reason Epic wins, and walks through why the June email is superseded). Distractor discipline: includes all three scenario distractors (voice-to-text, GDPR, no-show), two of them elaborated at paragraph length with no functional need - the task instructions call this a completeness illusion, not thoroughness. All five probes answerable from the document alone, but the missing FR/UX/target-user/open-questions sections mean the document could not actually be handed to a builder as-is despite the ask asking for exactly that.

result.rationale: Both documents correctly resolve every conflict the scenario poses (Epic over athenahealth, October 1 over the stale Q1 email, Carla Nguyen over the medical director on sequencing, patient-owned-device over full kiosk buildout) and both let a judge answer all five retrieval probes from the document alone, so neither fails on the scenario's core ask. The split is on document discipline and completeness. Artifact A carries the full PRD skeleton the rubric checks for - a dedicated, quantified Target users section, an FR table with a MoSCoW column on every row, an Open questions table with named owners and dated milestones, and an explicit Primary/Guardrail/Measurement-window split in Success metrics - and it stays disciplined about distractors, including only one of the scenario's three (voice-to-text, one line) and omitting GDPR and the no-show claim entirely. Artifact B is well-argued prose with slightly stronger held-out decision-traceability (it narrates *why* it decided things, not just what), but it drops three rubric-load-bearing sections outright - no Target users section, no FR list with priorities, no UX/unhappy-path content, no dated Open questions table - and it reproduces two of the scenario's three named distractors (GDPR, the no-show claim) at paragraph length, which the task instructions explicitly flag as a false-completeness signal to penalize rather than reward. The rubric-mean gap (3.83 vs 2.5) is a real content gap, not a structure-vs-substance illusion: the held-out mean gap runs the opposite direction (3.75 vs 3.5, roughly flat), which is exactly the circularity-control pattern the rubric describes as meaningful - A's rubric advantage reflects genuine missing deliverable content in B (no buildable FR list, no UX error states), not merely A performing the rubric's own checklist better.

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Strong structural completeness: FR table with MoSCoW priority, NFR table, Dependencies table with owner/status, Rollout plan, Open questions with named owners and milestone dates. Problem section is evidenced (12% reassignment rate, Denver double-booking recurrence) and outweighs the shorter Solution overview. Goals mix outcome metrics (build-time cut, delay cut in half) with a guardrail-flavored goal (zero rest-day violations), though there is no dedicated Success metrics section pairing a primary metric with a named guardrail and measurement window the way the rubric wants -- it has to be assembled from the Goals list. Target users section names the specific segment (regional scheduler, 9 hubs, 340 drivers) with situation. Two real weaknesses pull this down: (1) no UX and design section at all, so the unhappy-path half of that criterion is unmet even though FR priorities are present; (2) no explicit stop or kill condition anywhere in Risks or Rollout -- probe 2 is unanswerable from this document. It also includes one of the two scenario distractors (the long-haul trucking division non-goal), which the anti-form instruction says to penalize as reduced discipline rather than credit as thoroughness. Decision-vs-input traceability is middling: the VP's delay-cut target is attributed, but most other calls (DriverGo scope-out, pilot sequencing) are stated in flat authorial voice without marking them as the author's own judgment versus a stakeholder instruction.

artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: The strongest problem section of the three: names the scheduler (Renata Okafor), gives the 3-4 hour and 12% figures, and explicitly flags its own evidence quality ('a single data point from one region, not a company-wide measurement... worth treating as representative until we have more') rather than overstating certainty -- genuinely senior instinct. Target user section is equally specific, naming the same scheduler by name plus her situation. This document is the only one of the three with an explicit, named Stop condition section, and the only one with a dedicated Ownership section naming who validates the rest-day rule -- both held-out criteria the rubric and guide never teach, so their presence here is a real (not rubric-taught) signal. It is also the clearest at separating decision from input: it repeatedly marks facts as 'a signal, not a settled conclusion' and distinguishes what the VP set as a target from what the author is proposing as supporting metrics. Where it falls short of the ask is engineering-sizing scaffolding: there is no functional-requirements table with per-row MoSCoW priority, no dependencies table with owner and status columns (DriverGo and HR risk are discussed narratively but not tracked as sized, owned line items), no UX and design section with empty/loading/error states, and no Open Questions section at all -- so a reader cannot point to an owned, dated open question, which is a clean miss on that rubric criterion. It also carries the same long-haul-trucking distractor as Artifact A in its out-of-scope paragraph.

artifacts.label: Artifact C
artifacts.notes: Unfilled template: the title itself is a literal {{title}} placeholder, and every section is generic filler ('a meaningful improvement', 'the relevant users', 'as appropriate') with zero domain content -- no mention of drivers, schedulers, DriverGo, the union rest-day rule, the VP's target, or any number from the brief. Every rubric criterion fails outright: the single Goal is not a measurable outcome, the single Non-goal is a blank placeholder, the FR row and NFR row are untestable, the Open Questions row literally reads 'Certain aspects of this work remain to be finalized' with owner 'The appropriate owner' and date 'In due course', and there are no empty/loading/error states, just a paragraph asserting the UX 'has been designed with the user in mind.' None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document. It technically contains no internal contradiction and no distractor content, but only because it contains no actual claims to contradict or distinguish -- that is vacuous compliance, not quality, so it does not earn credit on the held-out criteria either.

result.strongest: Artifact B, on balance, though it is close with Artifact A and neither reaches a 4. B has the most evidenced problem section, the only explicit stop/kill condition, the only explicit ownership statement for the union rest-day rule, the clearest separation of stakeholder input from author judgment, and it is the only artifact that lets a judge answer all five retrieval probes from the document alone. A wins on engineering-sizing scaffolding (a prioritized FR table and an owner/status dependencies table that B lacks entirely), which matters for the ask's explicit 'engineering can size it' requirement, and that is the main thing keeping A competitive. Both A and B include the same long-haul-trucking distractor and are penalized for it. Artifact C is an unfilled template with zero domain content and fails every criterion and every probe.
result.rationale: I read the rubric (six rubric criteria drawn from the guide's self-grade checklist, four held-out criteria confirmed absent from the template/guide) and the full scenario, including its five retrieval probes and its two named distractors (the $50k finance budget-review trigger, and the long-haul trucking division exclusion). I scored each artifact by locating pointable evidence for each criterion directly in the text, checked each of the five probes against each document in isolation, and applied the anti-form instruction by treating structural completeness (tables, headings) as neutral and instead weighing whether specific facts, owners, dates, and metrics were actually present and non-vacuous. Artifact C was scored near-floor because it is a generic unfilled template with a literal {{title}} placeholder and no scenario-specific content at all -- it fails every criterion by absence, not by a close call. Artifacts A and B trade off: A is more complete as an engineering-sizing document (FR priorities, dependency owners/status, dated open questions) but omits a stop condition entirely and has a thinner, unlabeled success-metrics story; B is stronger on evidence discipline, ownership, stop condition, and decision-vs-input traceability (all held-out, non-taught criteria) and answers all five probes, but supplies no FR table, no dependencies table, and no open questions section at all, which are real gaps against the ask's 'engineering can size it' requirement. Both include the same long-haul-trucking distractor, which I penalized in both rather than crediting either for 'more complete' scoping. Neither reached a 4 (solid, shippable with a nitpick) because each has more than one substantive, non-trivial gap rather than a single nitpick, and per the rubric's tie-breaking instruction I broke toward the lower anchor level in each case.

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Strongest on the six named rubric axes: precise timestamps in a real timeline table, root causes each backed by named evidence (stale distribution list, orphaned code ownership, dead Slack route, unsafe failover procedure) with no cause pinned to a person, and an impact table with mostly hard numbers. Correctly omits both distractors (the $42k cost figure and the 'migration scheduled next quarter' detail never appear). Real gaps keep it off a 4: Action Items has no actual ticket IDs (all 'TBD') and owners are roles, not people; Trigger asserts three published criteria were met but never says where any of them were published, so it reads asserted rather than sourced. On the held-out axes it is notably weaker than its rubric score suggests: it names no stop/rollback/kill condition anywhere, and on the VP's actual question (one-off vendor problem or systemic) it does not render a judgment, it opens a 48-hour action item to 'assess... and report that judgment to the VP,' which ducks the analytical work the ask explicitly requested rather than doing it. Probe 4 (who decides, by when) is only half-answerable: the 48-hour window is present but the document assigns the assessment to the Payments Eng lead, not the VP, so 'who decides' is not cleanly recoverable from the text.

artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: Weakest of the three on named structure: there is no Trigger section at all (the closest it gets is restating 'third SLA miss in five months' twice without citing a pre-published criterion), and Action Items is prose bullets with no owner name, no ticket, no status field, so actions_are_tracked scores as low as Artifact C's. Timeline is embedded in narrative rather than a discrete checkable list and never states a completion time. But it is the only artifact that does the actual hard job the ask demanded: a dedicated section directly answers the VP's one-off-vs-systemic question with a reasoned position ('two of the three contributing failures... are decayed internal maturity, not vendor behavior') rather than deferring it to a future ticket, explicitly separates what is confirmed from what is not ('I do not yet have a confirmed root-cause writeup... the best current explanation, not a verified one'), and states a genuine escalation/kill threshold ('after the second SLA miss in six months, the incident automatically escalates to VP-level review... rather than waiting for a third'). Root causes are evidenced (channel rename, stale distribution list, four-month ownership gap) even though the evidence lives partly in the narrative section rather than restated per-row. Correctly excludes both distractors: no cost figure, and it engages the migration question the ask requires without importing the 'scheduled next quarter' distractor detail. Probe 4 is half-answerable: it clearly names the VP as decision-maker but never states the 48-hour deadline.

artifacts.label: Artifact C
artifacts.notes: Uniformly generic boilerplate: every section substitutes vague placeholder phrasing ('a subset of users and systems,' 'a period of time consistent with the severity,' 'a combination of factors') for any of the incident's actual facts. Contains zero timestamps, zero named systems, zero magnitudes, zero named root causes, zero real owners or tickets. It happens to avoid stating either distractor, but only because it states no facts at all, which is not discipline, it is absence of content. None of the five retrieval probes are answerable from this document; a reader given only this file could not reconstruct what happened, when, why detection was slow, what made it worse, or who owns the follow-up. This is the reference case for the anti-form warning: it has the same section headings as Artifact A but none of the substance, and should not be scored anywhere near it on that basis.

result.strongest: Artifact B, on balance, though the panel result is genuinely split by axis. Artifact A wins cleanly on the six rubric criteria (checkable timeline table, evidenced multi-cause root-cause table, measured impact), but Artifact B wins decisively on the held-out decision-usefulness criteria: it is the only document that renders an actual judgment on the VP's one-off-vs-systemic question instead of deferring it to a future ticket, the only one that states a concrete escalation/kill threshold, and the only one that consistently distinguishes reported fact from author judgment and flags what remains unconfirmed. Artifact A's Trigger section asserts published criteria without citing them and its Action Items table is tracking-shaped but empty (TBD tickets, role-not-person owners); Artifact B's Trigger section is simply absent and its Action Items are untracked prose. Both fall short of a 4 on strict rubric terms, but B does more of the job the ask actually specified.
result.rationale: Scored each artifact independently against the rubric's six named criteria and four held-out criteria on the 1-5 anchor scale (5 = a senior practitioner would not touch it, 4 = solid with a nitpick, ties broken downward), then separately verified each of the scenario's five retrieval probes against the document text alone, and checked for the presence of either seeded distractor (the $42,000 cost figure; the 'migration scheduled next quarter' detail). All three artifacts correctly withheld both distractors, so no scores were adjusted for distractor inclusion. Per the anti-form instruction, Artifact A's clean section-by-section structure (which it shares with Artifact C, the empty boilerplate document) was deliberately not treated as evidence of quality on its own; where Artifact A filled in a labeled section with real information it was credited, and where it filled a section with unsourced assertion (Trigger) or empty-but-shaped tracking fields (Action Items: TBD tickets, role owners) it was scored on the literal rubric text, not the presence of the table. Artifact B's lack of a labeled Trigger section and its untracked prose Action Items were scored as genuine rubric misses, not merely a style difference, since those are named rubric criteria; but its narrative sections were credited in full for the specific, evidenced content they contain even though it isn't formatted as a table. Artifact C was scored near-uniformly at the floor because every section substitutes generic template language for the incident's actual facts, leaving zero of the five probes answerable from the document alone.

artifacts.label: Artifact A
artifacts.notes: Rubric detail: summary_stands_alone=4 (cause, duration, resolution state all present in Summary, appropriately hedged); impact_is_measured=5 (clean table, every row has system/duration/magnitude); timeline_is_checkable=4 (table with approximate but derived timestamps, honestly flags itself as needing log reconciliation rather than presenting false precision); root_causes_evidenced=4 (table with two candidate causes each backed by named evidence -- vendor status page, open support case, failed repro -- no person blamed); trigger_is_own=3 (names the actual numeric thresholds met but explicitly declines to cite which published doc they live in, deferring to an action item -- partial credit, not full); actions_are_tracked=2 (six rows have Type/Owner/Status columns but every Ticket cell is 'TBD', so none is actually checkable against a tracker yet, which is the criterion's central ask). Held-out: scopable_without_meeting=3 (several items, e.g. the Android repro line, are sizeable cold; others like 'confirm and cite trigger criteria' are process busywork); names_a_stop_kill_condition=1 (no rollback/kill condition anywhere); no_internal_contradiction=5 (rigorously consistent -- every section restates 'not confirmed' rather than drifting toward certainty); decision_vs_information_distinguishable=3 (attributes the theory to 'the on-call engineer's working theory' and separately flags its own refusal to assert a citation, a real but partial separation of report vs. judgment). Cleanly avoids all three scenario distractors (no social sentiment, no billing incident, no churn-data mention). All 5 probes answerable correctly from this document alone, including the SLA miss and the Android ruled-in/out status. Holistic 3: disciplined and honest, but the all-TBD ticket column and the unresolved trigger citation are more than a nitpick for a document type whose whole job is checkable follow-through.

artifacts.label: Artifact B
artifacts.notes: Rubric detail: summary_stands_alone=2 ('What happened' states duration and implies resolution but never mentions cause status at all -- that's pushed entirely into the next section, which is exactly the deferral the criterion penalizes); impact_is_measured=4 (population/duration/magnitude numbers present in prose for both playback and tickets, just not tabulated); timeline_is_checkable=2 (no discrete timestamped event list at all -- only the start time plus two duration figures restated in prose, nothing a reader could check entry-by-entry against a log); root_causes_evidenced=4 (confidence-graded bullets -- confirmed/unconfirmed -- each with named evidence, arguably the clearest causal reasoning of the two documents); trigger_is_own=1 (no Trigger section or published-criterion citation anywhere, the criterion is simply untouched); actions_are_tracked=1 (five numbered action items, none has a named owner or ticket in the document itself -- owner/date assignment is explicitly deferred to 'the exec meeting', so nothing here is yet checkable outside the document). Held-out: scopable_without_meeting=3 (comparable specificity to A on a couple of items, e.g. the Android repro ask); names_a_stop_kill_condition=1 (no stop/rollback condition stated); no_internal_contradiction=4 (internally consistent, though the header status line never actually confirms the incident itself is resolved, only that root cause is unconfirmed -- a minor ambiguity, not a contradiction); decision_vs_information_distinguishable=5 (the explicit 'Confirmed, high confidence' / 'Unconfirmed, low confidence' labeling is the strongest report-vs-judgment separation of either document). All 5 probes answerable correctly, including the explicit 'we don't know' on the February linkage. Notably, B's 'explicitly out of scope' section names all three scenario distractors (social sentiment, the unrelated billing incident, pending churn data) by name in order to exclude them -- under the anti-form instruction this still counts as including distractor content rather than simply omitting it, and costs discipline points even though the intent was hygienic. Holistic 2: excellent exec-facing epistemic honesty, but three of six rubric rows (timeline, trigger, actions) fail outright rather than merely falling short, which is a structural problem for this document type, not a style choice.

result.strongest: Neither document is unambiguously stronger; they fail in different registers. Artifact A is the stronger document under this rubric (rubric mean 3.67 vs 2.33) because it attempts every required section -- timeline table, trigger sourcing, a structured action-tracking table -- even where it has to admit a gap (TBD tickets, no citation for the trigger doc), and it never touches any of the three distractors. Artifact B reads better as exec prose and wins on the held-out judgment-separation criterion by a wide margin (its confirmed/unconfirmed confidence labeling is genuinely the best writing of the two), but it omits the timeline and trigger sections entirely, never assigns an owner or ticket to a single action item inside the document, and undermines its own discipline by naming all three distractor facts in order to wave them off. If forced to pick one to ship as the actual postmortem record (as opposed to the Thursday narrative memo), Artifact A is closer to usable as-is.
result.rationale: Scored strictly against the rubric's six criteria and the four held-out decision-usefulness criteria, with anchors applied conservatively (ties broken downward) per the eval protocol. Checked all five retrieval probes against each document in isolation and cross-checked both documents against the scenario's three named distractors, penalizing any document that surfaced them even under a hygienic 'out of scope' framing, per the anti-form instruction. Table-based presentation in Artifact A was not credited beyond what its cells actually contained (e.g. its Ticket column of all-TBD entries was scored as failing actions_are_tracked despite the table's professional appearance), and Artifact B's prose-only sections were not penalized for lacking table structure where the underlying numbers were still checkable (impact) but were penalized where genuinely absent (timeline, trigger, action ownership)."
